title: Oil hits five-month high as global stocks wobble on AI fears; retail sales in Great Britain fall as shoppers cut back - as it happened
byline: Lauren Almeida, Mark Sweney, Richard Partington
excerpt: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news
content_html:
From

12h ago

Closing post

Time to wrap up…

Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to above $115 a barrel – its highest level since May.

The increase came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran.

Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall.

The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic.

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.

Shareholders in Baillie Gifford trust vote against US activist Saba

The Edinburgh home side has secured victory – again – in the latest big showdown in the world of investment trusts. For the third time, shareholders in Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent famous for its big bets on US tech and AI firms, have voted against a proposal from aggressive US hedge fund Saba Capital.

Saba wanted to install three nominees on the board and started with a near-30% stake, plus support from presumed sympathiser, Sessa Capital, another US fund, with 7.7%. But the big voting block wasn’t enough. Some 99.5% of independent shareholders in the Baillie Gifford fund – mainly small UK shareholders and UK institutions – backed the board. On an impressive 84% turn-out, the result was a 53:47 rejection of Saba’s place-men.

It was the result our financial editor, Nils Pratley, called for. Tell the Saba time-wasters to get lost, he argued here:

Tom Burnet, chair of the Baillie Gifford fund, is jubilant at the result – and clearly annoyed that Saba forced yet another vote.

Burnet said:

On behalf of the Board, I would like to pass our gratitude to our independent shareholders for their continued support.

Those shareholders have again delivered a clear and decisive verdict. They have overwhelmingly rejected Saba’s nominees. For the third time, they have also expressed their clear support for the current Board. Repeatedly revisiting matters on which almost all of our independent shareholders have plainly already expressed their view places an unnecessary burden on the Company, diverting management time and resources from the delivery of the Company’s strategy and the creation of long-term shareholder value and incurring significant costs.

Oil price climbs to $115; US stocks fall at the open

Oil prices are still climbing today – with Brent crude, the international benchmark, now up 1.8% to $115.14 a barrel.

Investors are sticking with their more cautious approach on Wall Street too – the Dow Jones industrial average has just fallen by 171.3 points, or 0.32%, at the open in New York. The S&P 500 fell 26.2 points, or 0.34%, at the open​, while the Nasdaq dropped 114.9 points, or 0.44%.

US stocks are poised to fall when the market opens later this afternoon, with futures for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq down.

Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, adds that the prospect of higher borrowing costs will unsettle investors betting on companies that are spending huge amounts on AI.

Investors have turned highly nervous again about the cost of the build out, and there’s likely to be little comeback today for tech stocks which have been severely tested this week. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.6% to 26,009 and the S&P 500 fell 1.2% [on Thursday]. Futures markets point to a muted start for Wall Street with few sparks of hope around to ignite a meaningful recovery.

Boom in weight-loss drugs could trigger drop in beer sales, Heineken says

Mark Sweney

Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.

The world’s second largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month warning that GLP-1 use – led by Ozempic and Wegovy – can reduce the desire to drink alcohol, which could lead to “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars.

The document, revealed by Reuters, warned that the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.

The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.

GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick, easy solution to rapid weight loss, with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.

Heineken, the world’s second largest brewer after AB InBev, said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits are evolving.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, says the biggest news is from S&P’s PMI data is the composite employment index rising above 50 for the first time since the 2024 budget.

He said:

The jobs balance rose to 50.5 from 48.9 in September, consistent with a 9K month-to-month payrolls gain in October. Solid growth is helping, probably alongside an easing drag from the payroll-tax hike.

…The steady recovery in jobs growth further undermines any case for waiting to hike rates. A November rate hike is a shoo-in, and we expect another rone in February. We are very close to adding a third hike in May or earlier. It’s a really close call, but at the margin, we hold off after weak consumer signals this morning. It would take little—small further energy price rises, a hawkish DMP—to push us to three hikes.

UK business activity growth accelerates to fastest since February

Some good news amid the doom and gloom this morning – UK business activity growth has accelerated to its fastest since February, helped by rebound in new orders, according to a survey published this morning.

The preliminary S&P Global UK composite purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 53.1 in October, higher than forecast and up from 52.0 in September.

A number of businesses cited a boost to sales from AI investment spending and rising demand for technology services, according to the survey. However, it found there will still many reports of sales being affected by geopolitical uncertainty and weak consumer confidence. Weaker demand was evident in the construction and real estate sectors in particular, it found.

But Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said that the survey also showed that businesses were taking on additional workers for the first time since hiring fell after the autumn budget of 2024.

There are reports of paused spending due to a lack of clarity on domestic economic policy in the run up to the budget, meaning the promising economic picture from the latest PMIs should provide an encouraging base for further robust economic growth through the winter months, barring any adverse surprises to businesses in the tax and spending review.

Geopolitics, and notably the potential for conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine to add to energy market volatility, are, however, clearly still unsettling many businesses, and cost of living concerns and broader fiscal worries are being compounded by the shift to higher borrowing costs.

Price pressures remain worryingly elevated, not only making a rate hike from the Bank of England at its upcoming policy meeting a near certainty but also likely shortening the odds of further rate hikes into 2027.”

It is red across the board in the European stock market this morning, though the falls are not steep. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 index is down 0.4%, while the French Cac 40 is down 0.7%. The German Dax is down by 0.6%.

The Stoxx 600, which tracks the biggest companies across the continent, has fallen by 0.4%.

While less red tape will be welcome news for small businesses, the chancellor is still facing pressure from bigger companies in the UK for more support.

Earlier this month some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.

Businesses have asked for a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay national insurance contributions (Nics) from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment.

They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.

Government says it will 'slash red tape' to save businesses £800m

The UK government has promised it will “slash red tape” for businesses, in reforms it claims will save firms across the country £800m in administrative and tariff costs per year.

The changes will make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses, it said.

It comes as pressure grows on prime minister Andy Burnham and chancellor John Healey to reduce the cost of doing business in the UK ahead of the budget next week.

The government has set itself a target of reducing the administrative burden of regulation on businesses by 25% by the end of the current parliament.

Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds are scheduled to meet with small business leaders at No 10 North today, where they are expected to accept recommendations from the Small Business Taskforce.

Burnham said in a statement:

It’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street.

So we’re getting government off their backs and giving businesses the breathing space to grow. Because when businesses succeed, they create good jobs, strengthen their communities and bring growth to every part of the country.”

Healey said:

British firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses.

That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said that the changes were a “welcome step towards giving smaller firms more time and headroom to focus on their businesses.”

The test now is delivery. Cutting unnecessary admin can free firms to invest, compete and grow – and business will want to see that ambition translated quickly into meaningful reductions in the burden they face.”

Brent crude hits $114 a barrel

And pressure continues to build this morning, with oil prices rising again. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is up 1% this morning to $114 a barrel – its highest level since May.

Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, points out that oil is now up by about 60% since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and up around 90% in the year so far.

Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.

Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, says fears are rising that American and Israeli forces will be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US mid-term elections.

At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still be fired.

Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries is adding to supply concerns. The deteriorating situation is once again fanning inflation fears, with companies unlikely to keep absorbing higher energy and freight costs. The longer the conflicts rage, the greater the chance of higher prices becoming more embedded in the economy, and that’s why bets have increased on central banks hiking rates more rapidly.

UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Covid as cost of living bites

Richard Partington

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said:

Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

Gloomy picture for retailers in Christmas quarter, economists warn

Economists are warning there could be more gloom ahead for retailers as they enter into the crucial final quarter of the year – which includes Christmas.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said:

October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner.

In itself, the 0.4% m/m fall in retail sales volumes in September (consensus -0.1%, CE 0.0%) isn’t bad as it followed a 0.7% m/m rise in August, which was revised up from the first estimate of 0.5% m/m. Admittedly, some of it was due to a 2.2% m/m rise in fuel sales as households topped up their tanks before fuel prices rose even further. They are unlikely to do the same in October. But equally, part of the 0.9% m/m fall in sales at clothing stores was due to the unusually mild weather limiting sales of the new autumn/winter ranges. Soft clothing sales also contributed to the 0.4% m/m drop in sales at supermarkets. Both may perform better in October. Either way, total sales rose by a decent 0.7% q/q in Q3 as a whole.

That all said, the plunge in the GfK measure of consumer confidence, from -13 in September to a six-month low of -24 in October, shows that rising fuel and utility prices, higher borrowing costs and the fear of tax rises in the budget are taking a bigger toll on households. On the face of it, that’s consistent with the annual growth rate of retail sales volumes slowing from 0.8% in September to well below 0%.

This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in Q4 and Q1. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, noted that fashion retailers had fared the worst in September, despite the warm weather.

Although all other retail categories saw sales rise year-on-year, rising petrol prices meant that consumers had to divert more of their spending on filling up their cars – over 30% more than last September - meaning less to spend on other things.

So, while retail prices, and grocery prices in particular, have remained subdued thanks to industry competition and the delayed pass-through of cost increases due to the conflict in the Middle East, the higher-than-expected inflation reported earlier this week will inevitably translate into less in shoppers’ pockets in the critical run-up to Christmas.

With most retailers’ sales coming in the last three months of the year, the upcoming peak season remains on a knife edge. This time last year, uncertainty surrounding the late budget at the end of November held back spending in the preceding two months. While that makes this year’s comparisons easier, retailers will be hoping that anything announced by the Chancellor this year does not add further to their cost of doing business nor dent consumers’ sentiment, which already seems to have fallen from the highs at the end of summer.”

Introduction: Global stocks wobble as AI fears grow

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.

A fresh wave of selling hit AI stocks around the world overnight, as investor grow increasingly anxious around the sustainability of AI-fuelled returns.

The Japanese and South Korean stock markets, which have been buoyed up by their exposure to the AI investment boom, fell before recovering some ground to trade broadly flat on the day.

And over in the US, the blue chip S&P 500 fell by 1.2%, its worst performance since July, and the tech heavy Nasdaq dropped by 2.6%, its biggest drop since June. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell by a painful 6.7%, also its worst day since June.

Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, says our gloomy weather is reflected in the stock market:

As storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020.

Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl.

So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024.

And in a further sign that investors are taking a decidedly more conservative approach – there has been a strong move towards US Treasuries, widely considered the best quality government debt in the market and a safe haven asset. Reid says:

…In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%.

Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). And in turn, that pushed the smoother 4-week moving average to its lowest since September 2022, back when the unemployment rate was just 3.5%.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya, an analyst at Swissquote, says that the falling value of some of the biggest tech and AI stocks in the world suggests that the bubble in the sector is bursting.

Given the more than 50% retreat in memory chipmakers’ share prices from their peaks, we could now argue that their exponential rise was a bubble, and that the bubble has burst.

These memory chip companies continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand, and they’re trading at very low forward earnings multiples: Samsung and SK Hynix at around 3–4× — yes, 3–4 times! Alas, buyers are nowhere to be found.

Investors will be watching closely next week as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Sandisk are all due to report their latest results.

Elsewhere this morning, British retail sales fell by ⁠0.4% in September, compared with expectations of a drop of 0.1%.

An unseasonably warm start to the autumn weighed on ⁠online clothing vendors ⁠and ​supermarkets also saw a drop in volumes, official figures showed on Friday.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said:

The drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end.

At least part of the drop in retail sales in September can be attributed to warm weather dampening demand for winter clothing, which might reverse in October.

But retailers also reported lower footfall and customers cutting back, suggesting cost of living pressures might be starting to bite. Indeed, the slump in consumer confidence in October suggests that higher inflation and borrowing costs are now having a bigger impact on confidence and spending. Nervousness ahead of what seems likely to be another tax raising budget, may also be playing a role.

So we’re getting government off their backs and giving businesses the breathing space to grow. Because when businesses succeed, they create good jobs, strengthen their communities and bring growth to every part of the country.” Healey said: double quotation markBritish firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses. That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.” Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said that the changes were a “welcome step towards giving smaller firms more time and headroom to focus on their businesses.” double quotation markThe test now is delivery. Cutting unnecessary admin can free firms to invest, compete and grow – and business will want to see that ambition translated quickly into meaningful reductions in the burden they face.” Brent crude hits $114 a barrelFlames burn off at an oil processing facility in Saudi Aramco's oilfield in the Rub' Al-Khali desert in Shaybah, Saudi Arabia, on Tuesday, Oct. 2, 2018 Photograph: Simon Dawson/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAnd pressure continues to build this morning, with oil prices rising again. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is up 1% this morning to $114 a barrel – its highest level since May.Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, points out that oil is now up by about 60% since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and up around 90% in the year so far. double quotation markWidespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month. Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, says fears are rising that American and Israeli forces will be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US mid-term elections. double quotation markAt the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still be fired. Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries is adding to supply concerns. The deteriorating situation is once again fanning inflation fears, with companies unlikely to keep absorbing higher energy and freight costs. The longer the conflicts rage, the greater the chance of higher prices becoming more embedded in the economy, and that’s why bets have increased on central banks hiking rates more rapidly. In itself, the 0.4% m/m fall in retail sales volumes in September (consensus -0.1%, CE 0.0%) isn’t bad as it followed a 0.7% m/m rise in August, which was revised up from the first estimate of 0.5% m/m. Admittedly, some of it was due to a 2.2% m/m rise in fuel sales as households topped up their tanks before fuel prices rose even further. They are unlikely to do the same in October. But equally, part of the 0.9% m/m fall in sales at clothing stores was due to the unusually mild weather limiting sales of the new autumn/winter ranges. Soft clothing sales also contributed to the 0.4% m/m drop in sales at supermarkets. Both may perform better in October. Either way, total sales rose by a decent 0.7% q/q in Q3 as a whole. That all said, the plunge in the GfK measure of consumer confidence, from -13 in September to a six-month low of -24 in October, shows that rising fuel and utility prices, higher borrowing costs and the fear of tax rises in the budget are taking a bigger toll on households. On the face of it, that’s consistent with the annual growth rate of retail sales volumes slowing from 0.8% in September to well below 0%. This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in Q4 and Q1. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon. While that makes this year’s comparisons easier, retailers will be hoping that anything announced by the Chancellor this year does not add further to their cost of doing business nor dent consumers’ sentiment, which already seems to have fallen from the highs at the end of summer.” Introduction: Global stocks wobble as AI fears growGood morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy.A fresh wave of selling hit AI stocks around the world overnight, as investor grow increasingly anxious around the sustainability of AI-fuelled returns.The Japanese and South Korean stock markets, which have been buoyed up by their exposure to the AI investment boom, fell before recovering some ground to trade broadly flat on the day.And over in the US, the blue chip S&P 500 fell by 1.2%, its worst performance since July, and the tech heavy Nasdaq dropped by 2.6%, its biggest drop since June. The Philadelphia semiconductor index fell by a painful 6.7%, also its worst day since June.Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, says our gloomy weather is reflected in the stock market: double quotation markAs storm Austen hits these shores this morning, clouds kept darkening for markets yesterday, as the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once. First, there was mounting stress around France, with the Franco-German 10yr spread (+14.8bps) seeing its biggest daily widening since the initial pandemic turmoil in March 2020. Second, AI fears continued to gather pace, with the Philly semiconductor index (-6.72%) falling to its lowest level since July, which dragged down equities more broadly. And third, the latest geopolitical fears meant oil prices kept rising as well, with Brent crude (+4.00%) hitting a 5-month high of $113.17/bbl. So collectively, those concerns drove a huge risk-off move, with the 10yr Treasury yield (-16.6bps to 4.95%) seeing its biggest daily decline since August 2024. And in a further sign that investors are taking a decidedly more conservative approach – there has been a strong move towards US Treasuries, widely considered the best quality government debt in the market and a safe haven asset. Reid says: double quotation mark…In the midst of all these market pressures, an interesting theme was the flight to US Treasuries, which returned to its traditional risk-off role in periods of turmoil. In fact, the 10yr yield fell -16.6bps to 4.95%. Moreover, that came despite some strong US data, demonstrating how the financial stress was weighing on sentiment rather than the fundamentals. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to a 3-month low of 194k in the week ending October 17 (vs. 200k expected). And in turn, that pushed the smoother 4-week moving average to its lowest since September 2022, back when the unemployment rate was just 3.5%. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, an analyst at Swissquote, says that the falling value of some of the biggest tech and AI stocks in the world suggests that the bubble in the sector is bursting. double quotation markGiven the more than 50% retreat in memory chipmakers’ share prices from their peaks, we could now argue that their exponential rise was a bubble, and that the bubble has burst. These memory chip companies continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand, and they’re trading at very low forward earnings multiples: Samsung and SK Hynix at around 3–4× — yes, 3–4 times! Alas, buyers are nowhere to be found. Investors will be watching closely next week as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Sandisk are all due to report their latest results.Elsewhere this morning, British retail sales fell by ⁠0.4% in September, compared with expectations of a drop of 0.1%. An unseasonably warm start to the autumn weighed on ⁠online clothing vendors ⁠and ​supermarkets also saw a drop in volumes, official figures showed on Friday.Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: double quotation markThe drop in retail sales in September and sharp fall in consumer confidence in October raises the risk that the economy’s recent run of resilience might be coming to an end. At least part of the drop in retail sales in September can be attributed to warm weather dampening demand for winter clothing, which might reverse in October. But retailers also reported lower footfall and customers cutting back, suggesting cost of living pressures might be starting to bite. Indeed, the slump in consumer confidence in October suggests that higher inflation and borrowing costs are now having a bigger impact on confidence and spending. Nervousness ahead of what seems likely to be another tax raising budget, may also be playing a role. blocks.html_en: Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said:

sentences.en: Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said:

blocks.html_en:
October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner.

In itself, the 0.4% m/m fall in retail sales volumes in September (consensus -0.1%, CE 0.0%) isn’t bad as it followed a 0.7% m/m rise in August, which was revised up from the first estimate of 0.5% m/m. Admittedly, some of it was due to a 2.2% m/m rise in fuel sales as households topped up their tanks before fuel prices rose even further. They are unlikely to do the same in October. But equally, part of the 0.9% m/m fall in sales at clothing stores was due to the unusually mild weather limiting sales of the new autumn/winter ranges. Soft clothing sales also contributed to the 0.4% m/m drop in sales at supermarkets. Both may perform better in October. Either way, total sales rose by a decent 0.7% q/q in Q3 as a whole.

That all said, the plunge in the GfK measure of consumer confidence, from -13 in September to a six-month low of -24 in October, shows that rising fuel and utility prices, higher borrowing costs and the fear of tax rises in the budget are taking a bigger toll on households. On the face of it, that’s consistent with the annual growth rate of retail sales volumes slowing from 0.8% in September to well below 0%.

This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in Q4 and Q1. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.

是时候结束了……

Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to above $115 a barrel – its highest level since May.

The increase came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran.

Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall.

The decrease, which was fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of an unseasonably warm September, comes as figures show consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic.

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.

Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.

Shareholders in Baillie Gifford trust vote against US activist Saba

The Edinburgh home side has secured victory – again – in the latest big showdown in the world of investment trusts. For the third time, shareholders in Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, a FTSE 250 constituent famous for its big bets on US tech and AI firms, have voted against a proposal from aggressive US hedge fund Saba Capital.

Saba wanted to install three nominees on the board and started with a near-30% stake, plus support from presumed sympathiser, Sessa Capital, another US fund, with 7.7%. But the big voting block wasn’t enough. Some 99.5% of independent shareholders in the Baillie Gifford fund – mainly small UK shareholders and UK institutions – backed the board. On an impressive 84% turn-out, the result was a 53:47 rejection of Saba’s place-men.

It was the result our financial editor, Nils Pratley, called for. Tell the Saba time-wasters to get lost, he argued here:

Tom Burnet, chair of the Baillie Gifford fund, is jubilant at the result – and clearly annoyed that Saba forced yet another vote.

Burnet said:

double quotation markOn behalf of the Board, I would like to pass our gratitude to our independent shareholders for their continued support. Those shareholders have again delivered a clear and decisive verdict. They have overwhelmingly rejected Saba’s nominees. For the third time, they have also expressed their clear support for the current Board. Repeatedly revisiting matters on which almost all of our independent shareholders have plainly already expressed their view places an unnecessary burden on the Company, diverting management time and resources from the delivery of the Company’s strategy and the creation of long-term shareholder value and incurring significant costs.

Oil price climbs to $115; US stocks fall at the open

Oil prices are still climbing today – with Brent crude, the international benchmark, now up 1.8% to $115.14 a barrel.

Investors are sticking with their more cautious approach on Wall Street too – the Dow Jones industrial average has just fallen by 171.3 points, or 0.32%, at the open in New York. The S&P 500 fell 26.2 points, or 0.34%, at the open​, while the Nasdaq dropped 114.9 points, or 0.44%.

US stocks are poised to fall when the market opens later this afternoon, with futures for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq down.

Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, adds that the prospect of higher borrowing costs will unsettle investors betting on companies that are spending huge amounts on AI.

double quotation markInvestors have turned highly nervous again about the cost of the build out, and there’s likely to be little comeback today for tech stocks which have been severely tested this week. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 2.6% to 26,009 and the S&P 500 fell 1.2% [on Thursday]. Futures markets point to a muted start for Wall Street with few sparks of hope around to ignite a meaningful recovery.

Boom in weight-loss drugs could trigger drop in beer sales, Heineken says

Mark Sweney

Heineken has warned British bars and pubs that the boom in popularity of weight-loss drugs could lead to a fall in sales of beer and cider.

The world’s second largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month warning that GLP-1 use – led by Ozempic and Wegovy – can reduce the desire to drink alcohol, which could lead to “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars.

The document, revealed by Reuters, warned that the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.

The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.

GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick, easy solution to rapid weight loss, with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.

Heineken, the world’s second largest brewer after AB InBev, said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits are evolving.

Rob Wood, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, says the biggest news is from S&P’s PMI data is the composite employment index rising above 50 for the first time since the 2024 budget.

他说：

double quotation markThe jobs balance rose to 50.5 from 48.9 in September, consistent with a 9K month-to-month payrolls gain in October. Solid growth is helping, probably alongside an easing drag from the payroll-tax hike. …The steady recovery in jobs growth further undermines any case for waiting to hike rates. A November rate hike is a shoo-in, and we expect another rone in February. We are very close to adding a third hike in May or earlier. It’s a really close call, but at the margin, we hold off after weak consumer signals this morning. It would take little—small further energy price rises, a hawkish DMP—to push us to three hikes.

UK business activity growth accelerates to fastest since February

Some good news amid the doom and gloom this morning – UK business activity growth has accelerated to its fastest since February, helped by rebound in new orders, according to a survey published this morning.

The preliminary S&P Global UK composite purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 53.1 in October, higher than forecast and up from 52.0 in September.

A number of businesses cited a boost to sales from AI investment spending and rising demand for technology services, according to the survey. However, it found there will still many reports of sales being affected by geopolitical uncertainty and weak consumer confidence. Weaker demand was evident in the construction and real estate sectors in particular, it found.

But Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said that the survey also showed that businesses were taking on additional workers for the first time since hiring fell after the autumn budget of 2024.

double quotation markThere are reports of paused spending due to a lack of clarity on domestic economic policy in the run up to the budget, meaning the promising economic picture from the latest PMIs should provide an encouraging base for further robust economic growth through the winter months, barring any adverse surprises to businesses in the tax and spending review. Geopolitics, and notably the potential for conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine to add to energy market volatility, are, however, clearly still unsettling many businesses, and cost of living concerns and broader fiscal worries are being compounded by the shift to higher borrowing costs. Price pressures remain worryingly elevated, not only making a rate hike from the Bank of England at its upcoming policy meeting a near certainty but also likely shortening the odds of further rate hikes into 2027.”

It is red across the board in the European stock market this morning, though the falls are not steep. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 index is down 0.4%, while the French Cac 40 is down 0.7%. The German Dax is down by 0.6%.

The Stoxx 600, which tracks the biggest companies across the continent, has fallen by 0.4%.

While less red tape will be welcome news for small businesses, the chancellor is still facing pressure from bigger companies in the UK for more support.

Earlier this month some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget.

Businesses have asked for a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay national insurance contributions (Nics) from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment.

They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets.

Government says it will 'slash red tape' to save businesses £800m

The UK government has promised it will “slash red tape” for businesses, in reforms it claims will save firms across the country £800m in administrative and tariff costs per year.

The changes will make compliance guidance clearer, simplify the UK’s corporate reporting requirements and extend import tariff suspensions on products favoured by businesses, it said.

It comes as pressure grows on prime minister Andy Burnham and chancellor John Healey to reduce the cost of doing business in the UK ahead of the budget next week.

The government has set itself a target of reducing the administrative burden of regulation on businesses by 25% by the end of the current parliament.

Burnham and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds are scheduled to meet with small business leaders at No 10 North today, where they are expected to accept recommendations from the Small Business Taskforce.

Burnham said in a statement:

double quotation markIt’s not right that pointless bureaucracy gets in the way of people working hard to build something that matters to their high street. So we’re getting government off their backs and giving businesses the breathing space to grow. Because when businesses succeed, they create good jobs, strengthen their communities and bring growth to every part of the country.”

Healey said:

double quotation markBritish firms are fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork that eats into valuable time and money when they simply want to get on with running their businesses. That is why we are cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and giving businesses the breathing space they need to invest, innovate and create good jobs.”

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry (CBI), said that the changes were a “welcome step towards giving smaller firms more time and headroom to focus on their businesses.”

double quotation markThe test now is delivery. Cutting unnecessary admin can free firms to invest, compete and grow – and business will want to see that ambition translated quickly into meaningful reductions in the burden they face.”

Brent crude hits $114 a barrel

And pressure continues to build this morning, with oil prices rising again. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, is up 1% this morning to $114 a barrel – its highest level since May.

Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, points out that oil is now up by about 60% since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and up around 90% in the year so far.

double quotation markWidespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.

Susannah Streeter, of the broker Wealth Club, says fears are rising that American and Israeli forces will be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US mid-term elections.

double quotation markAt the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still be fired. Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries is adding to supply concerns. UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Covid as cost of living bites

Richard Partington

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said:

double quotation markRelentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

Gloomy picture for retailers in Christmas quarter, economists warn

Economists are warning there could be more gloom ahead for retailers as they enter into the crucial final quarter of the year – which includes Christmas.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said:

double quotation markOctober’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner. In itself, the 0.4% m/m fall in retail sales volumes in September (consensus -0.1%, CE 0.0%) isn’t bad as it followed a 0.7% m/m rise in August, which was revised up from the first estimate of 0.5% m/m. Admittedly, some of it was due to a 2.2% m/m rise in fuel sales as households topped up their tanks before fuel prices rose even further. They are unlikely to do the same in October. But equally, part of the 0.9% m/m fall in sales at clothing stores was due to the unusually mild weather limiting sales of the new autumn/winter ranges. Soft clothing sales also contributed to the 0.4% m/m drop in sales at supermarkets. Both may perform better in October. Either way, total sales rose by a decent 0.7% q/q in Q3 as a whole. That all said, the plunge in the GfK measure of consumer confidence, from -13 in September to a six-month low of -24 in October, shows that rising fuel and utility prices, higher borrowing costs and the fear of tax rises in the budget are taking a bigger toll on households. On the face of it, that’s consistent with the annual growth rate of retail sales volumes slowing from 0.8% in September to well below 0%. This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in Q4 and Q1. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.

Jacqueline Windsor, head of retail at PwC UK, noted that fashion retailers had fared the worst in September, despite the warm weather.

double quotation markAlthough all other retail categories saw sales rise year-on-year, rising petrol prices meant that consumers had to divert more of their spending on filling up their cars – over 30% more than last September - meaning less to spend on other things. So, while retail prices, and grocery prices in particular, have remained subdued thanks to industry competition and the delayed pass-through of cost increases due to the conflict in the Middle East, the higher-than-expected inflation reported earlier this week will inevitably translate into less in shoppers’ pockets in the critical run-up to Christmas. With most retailers’ sales coming in the last three months of the year, the upcoming peak season remains on a knife edge. This time last year, uncertainty surrounding the late budget at the end of November held back spending in the preceding two months. While that makes this year’s comparisons easier, retailers will be hoping that anything announced by the Chancellor this year does not add further to their cost of doing business nor dent consumers’ sentiment, which already seems to have fallen from the highs at the end of summer.”
